o: Cut an m×n board with full-length horizontal/vertical cuts into pieces whose shapes have listed prices; maximize revenue (no rotation allowed). With m,n ≤ 200, define dp[i][j] = best revenue from an i×j piece: either sell it whole (if priced), or split at some row or column and combine the two optimal sub-pieces. Example 1: 3×5 splits into two 2×2 (14), a 2×1 (3), and a 1×4 (2) → 19. The recurrence explores O(m+n) cuts per cell → ~1.6e7 operations, comfortably fast.
k: Optimal substructure: any first cut divides the piece into two independent subproblems.
dp[i][j] = max(direct price, max over horizontal cuts, max over vertical cuts); halving the cut range (cut at c, pieces c and i−c) avoids double work.
Memoized top-down and bottom-up tabulation are equivalent; tabulation avoids recursion overhead.

a.i: Fill dp in increasing order of dimensions so sub-pieces are ready when needed. Store prices in a hash map keyed by (h, w) or a 2D price table.
s: Initialize price lookup from the prices list.
For i = 1..m, j = 1..n: start with the whole-piece price (or 0); try all horizontal cuts c < i and vertical cuts c < j; take the max.
a.t: O(m·n·(m+n)) ≈ 200·200·400 = 1.6e7 — three nested loops per cell.
a.sp: O(m·n) for the DP and price tables.

a.i: Same recurrence expressed recursively on (i, j) with a memo dictionary; often easier to reason about and only touches reachable states (all of them here, but the pattern extends to sparse constraints).
s: Define solve(i, j) returning dp value; cache results.
Base: 0 for empty dims; seed with the direct price.
a.t: O(m·n·(m+n)) — each state computed once with O(m+n) transitions.
a.sp: O(m·n) memo plus O(m+n) recursion stack.

w: Bottom-up is preferred in interviews (no recursion-depth concerns). Pitfalls: forgetting the whole-piece sale option, iterating cuts over the full range instead of half (only a constant factor, but shows insight), and no-rotation meaning dp[i][j] ≠ dp[j][i]. Follow-ups: cutting costs per cut, limited inventory of salable shapes, or 3D blocks.
